title: Acid–base concepts
competency: Define acids and bases by the Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis concepts, identify conjugate pairs and amphiprotic species.

keywords.def: A substance that increases [H⁺] (H₃O⁺) when dissolved in water.
A substance that increases [OH⁻] when dissolved in water.
Two species that differ by exactly one H⁺, such as HF and F⁻.
Two identical molecules react to give a cation and an anion: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
A molecule or ion that can donate or accept a proton, depending on its partner.
A species that accepts an electron pair to form a bond.
A species that donates an electron pair to form a bond.

en.text: Arrhenius defined acids and bases by what they do in water. An acid increases [H⁺] (really H₃O⁺); a base increases [OH⁻]. Strong acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄) and strong bases (Group 1 hydroxides, Ca, Sr and Ba hydroxides) ionize completely. The idea fails outside water and for bases such as NH₃ that contain no OH.

am.text: አርሄኒየስ አሲድ በውሃ ውስጥ [H⁺] ይጨምራል፤ ቤዝ [OH⁻] ይጨምራል። ሀሳቡ ከውሃ ውጭ እና እንደ NH₃ ላሉ ቤዞች አይሠራም።

screens.title: Lemon or soap?
screens.ask: Almaz dips blue litmus paper into four liquids. Which one turns it red?
screens.after:
Lemon juice contains citric acid, so it is acidic.
Acids turn blue litmus red.
Soap and ammonia solutions are basic: they turn red litmus blue.
Salt water is neutral: no change.

screens.title: Arrhenius acids and bases
paras: An acid increases [H⁺] in water. A base increases [OH⁻].
H⁺ never exists alone in water. It joins H₂O to form H₃O⁺.
Strong acid: ionizes completely. HClO₄ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + ClO₄⁻.
Strong acids: HCl, HBr, HI, HNO₃, H₂SO₄, HClO₄.
Strong bases: Group 1 hydroxides and Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂.
Neutralization: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

screens.title: The strong ones
screens.ask: Tap each card. Strong acids and bases ionize completely in water.
items: HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻. One arrow: every molecule ionizes.
HNO₃ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + NO₃⁻. A strong acid.
H₂SO₄ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + HSO₄⁻. The first H⁺ leaves completely.
HClO₄ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + ClO₄⁻. The book's example.
NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻. Group 1 hydroxides are strong bases.
Ba(OH)₂ → Ba²⁺ + 2OH⁻. Two OH⁻ per formula unit.

screens.title: Where Arrhenius fails
paras: It works only in water.
NH₃ and Na₂CO₃ make water basic but contain no OH⁻ to release.
It cannot explain HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s), which happens without water.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A substance that increases [H⁺] (H₃O⁺) when dissolved in water.
A substance that increases [OH⁻] when dissolved in water.

screens.title: Classify by Arrhenius
screens.why:
Step 1: ask which ion each substance releases in water.
Step 2: HBr and HNO₃ release H⁺ (as H₃O⁺): Arrhenius acids.
Step 3: NaOH and KOH release OH⁻: Arrhenius bases.
Step 4: NaCl gives only Na⁺ and Cl⁻: neither.
Check: an acid formula starts with H; a base here ends in OH.
screens.clue: What ion does each give in water?
screens.text: Sort each substance by what it adds to water.
True or false: a bare H⁺ ion moves freely in water.
screens.why:
Step 1: H⁺ is a bare proton with no electrons.
Step 2: Water has lone pairs on its O atom.
Step 3: The proton bonds at once to one lone pair: H⁺ + H₂O → H₃O⁺.
So the statement is false. We write H⁺(aq) only as a shorthand for H₃O⁺.
screens.clue: What happens when a proton meets a lone pair on water?

screens.text: Arrhenius limits: which is a drawback of the Arrhenius concept?
opts: It cannot explain why NH₃ is a base
It cannot explain why HCl is an acid
It cannot explain why NaOH is a base
It cannot explain neutralization in water
screens.ans: It cannot explain why NH₃ is a base
screens.why:
Step 1: an Arrhenius base must release OH⁻ in water.
Step 2: NH₃ has no OH in its formula.
Step 3: Yet NH₃ solution is basic, so Arrhenius cannot explain it.
HCl, NaOH and neutralization in water fit Arrhenius well, so those options are not drawbacks.
screens.clue: Look for the base without OH in its formula.

screens.text: Arrhenius limits: which reaction can the Arrhenius concept NOT describe as acid–base?
screens.why:
Step 1: Arrhenius needs water and ions (H⁺, OH⁻).
Step 2: HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄Cl(s) happens in the gas phase.
Step 3: There is no water and no OH⁻.
So Arrhenius cannot call it acid–base. The other three all happen in water.
screens.clue: Which one happens in the gas phase?

ideas.name: Brønsted–Lowry acids, bases and conjugate pairs

en.text: Brønsted and Lowry (1923) defined an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor, in any medium. When an acid gives up H⁺ it becomes its conjugate base; when a base takes H⁺ it becomes its conjugate acid. The partners differ by one H⁺. The stronger an acid, the weaker its conjugate base, and reactions favour the weaker acid and weaker base.

am.text: ብሮንስቴድ–ሎውሪ፡ አሲድ ፕሮቶን ሰጪ፣ ቤዝ ፕሮቶን ተቀባይ ነው። ተጓዳኝ ጥንዶች በአንድ H⁺ ይለያያሉ። ጠንካራ አሲድ ደካማ ተጓዳኝ ቤዝ አለው።

screens.title: Who gives the proton?
screens.ask: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. Which reactant gives away a proton (H⁺)?
screens.after:
Compare each reactant with its product.
H₂O loses one H⁺ and becomes OH⁻: water is the proton donor (acid).
NH₃ gains that H⁺ and becomes NH₄⁺: ammonia is the proton acceptor (base).

screens.title: Proton donors and acceptors
paras: Acid: proton donor. Base: proton acceptor.
Water is not needed.
NH₃ is a base because it accepts H⁺ from water.
Every Arrhenius acid is also a Brønsted–Lowry acid.

screens.title: Conjugate pairs
paras: Acid − H⁺ → its conjugate base. Base + H⁺ → its conjugate acid.
The conjugate base has one fewer H and one more minus charge.

screens.title: Find the two conjugate pairs
steps: Write the reaction: HF + H₂O ⇌ F⁻ + H₃O⁺.
HF loses one H⁺ and becomes F⁻. HF is the acid.
H₂O gains that H⁺ and becomes H₃O⁺. H₂O is the base.
Pair 1: HF (acid) and F⁻ (its conjugate base).
Check: each pair differs by exactly one H⁺.

screens.title: Strength of conjugate pairs
paras: The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
HCl is strong, so Cl⁻ is a negligible base.
Reactions go mainly toward the weaker acid and weaker base.
Tap the cards below: strongest acid first (Chart 1.1).

screens.title: Acid strength and base strength
screens.ask: Tap each acid, from strongest to weakest. Watch its conjugate base get stronger.
items: Its conjugate base Cl⁻ is negligible. It never takes H⁺ back in water.
Its conjugate base is H₂O, a very weak base.
Its conjugate base is F⁻, a weak base.
Its conjugate base is CH₃COO⁻, a weak base, stronger than F⁻.
Its conjugate base is NH₃, a weak base, stronger than CH₃COO⁻.
Its conjugate base is OH⁻, a strong base.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Two species that differ by exactly one H⁺, such as HF and F⁻.

screens.text: Conjugate pairs: what is the conjugate acid of HPO₄²⁻?
screens.why:
Step 1: a conjugate acid has one MORE H⁺ than the base.
Step 2: add one H: HPO₄ → H₂PO₄.
Step 3: fix the charge: −2 + 1 = −1.
Answer: H₂PO₄⁻. H₃PO₄ adds two H⁺; PO₄³⁻ removes one.
screens.clue: Add exactly one H⁺ and fix the charge.

screens.title: Match each acid with its conjugate base
screens.why:
Step 1: an acid gives away one H⁺ to form its conjugate base.
Step 2: so remove one H and make the charge one more negative.
Step 3: HF → F⁻, NH₄⁺ → NH₃, H₂O → OH⁻.
Step 4: HCO₃⁻ → CO₃²⁻, H₂PO₄⁻ → HPO₄²⁻.
Check: each pair differs by exactly one H⁺.
screens.clue: One fewer H, one more minus.

screens.text: Find the Brønsted–Lowry acid (proton donor) in OCl⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HOCl + OH⁻.
screens.why:
Step 1: compare each reactant with the products.
Step 2: OCl⁻ gains H⁺ and becomes HOCl: OCl⁻ is the base.
Step 3: H₂O loses H⁺ and becomes OH⁻: H₂O is the acid.
Answer: H₂O. HOCl and OH⁻ are products, the conjugate acid and base.

screens.text: Conjugate pairs: which of these is NOT a conjugate acid–base pair?
screens.why:
Step 1: a conjugate pair differs by exactly one H⁺.
Step 2: H₃O⁺ has 3 H; OH⁻ has 1 H. They differ by two H⁺.
Step 3: the real pairs are H₃O⁺/H₂O and H₂O/OH⁻.
NH₃/NH₄⁺, HS⁻/H₂S and NH₃/NH₂⁻ each differ by one H⁺, so they are pairs.
screens.clue: Count the H atoms in each pair.

screens.text: Use Ka to rank conjugate bases. Ka: HF 7.2 × 10⁻⁴, HNO₂ 4.5 × 10⁻⁴, HCN 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁰. Order F⁻, NO₂⁻, CN⁻ by base strength, strongest first:
screens.why:
Step 1: rank the acids by Ka: HF > HNO₂ > HCN.
Step 2: a stronger acid has a weaker conjugate base.
Step 3: so reverse the order for the bases.
Answer: CN⁻ > NO₂⁻ > F⁻.
Trap: do not copy the acid order; F⁻ is the WEAKEST base here.
screens.clue: Reverse the order of the acids.

screens.title: Put these bases in order, strongest first
screens.why:
Step 1: write each base's conjugate acid: H₂O, NH₄⁺, CH₃COOH, HNO₃, HCl.
Step 2: rank the acids, weakest first: H₂O < NH₄⁺ < CH₃COOH < HNO₃ < HCl.
Step 3: the weakest acid has the strongest conjugate base.
Answer: OH⁻ > NH₃ > CH₃COO⁻ > NO₃⁻ > Cl⁻.
screens.clue: The weaker the conjugate acid, the stronger the base.
screens.text: Rank these Brønsted–Lowry bases by strength, strongest first.

en.text: Some species can donate or accept a proton depending on their partner: they are amphiprotic. Water is the most important one; HCO₃⁻ and H₂PO₄⁻ are others. In autoionization two identical molecules transfer a proton: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ and 2NH₃ ⇌ NH₄⁺ + NH₂⁻.

am.text: አምፊፕሮቲክ ዝርያዎች እንደ አጋራቸው ፕሮቶን ይሰጣሉ ወይም ይቀበላሉ፤ ውሃ ዋናው ምሳሌ ነው። 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻።

screens.title: Acid or base?
screens.ask: Water reacts with NH₃ and with CH₃COOH. What role does water play?
opts: A base with CH₃COOH, an acid with NH₃
screens.after:
With acetic acid, water accepts H⁺ and becomes H₃O⁺: it is a base.
With ammonia, water gives H⁺ and becomes OH⁻: it is an acid.
So water's role depends on its partner.
screens.best: A base with CH₃COOH, an acid with NH₃

screens.title: Autoionization
paras: Two identical molecules react to give a cation and an anion.
Water: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
One molecule acts as an acid, the other as a base.
Liquid ammonia: 2NH₃ ⇌ NH₄⁺ + NH₂⁻.

screens.title: Water plays both roles
steps: Two water molecules meet: H₂O + H₂O.
One molecule gives an H⁺. It becomes OH⁻. It is the acid.
The other takes that H⁺ with a lone pair. It becomes H₃O⁺. It is the base.
Net: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻. This is autoionization.
Liquid ammonia does the same: 2NH₃ ⇌ NH₄⁺ + NH₂⁻.

screens.title: Amphiprotic species
paras: They can donate or accept a proton.
HCO₃⁻ + OH⁻ → CO₃²⁻ + H₂O: HCO₃⁻ is an acid.
HCO₃⁻ + HF → H₂CO₃ + F⁻: HCO₃⁻ is a base.
Other examples: H₂O, H₂PO₄⁻, HPO₄²⁻, HS⁻.

screens.title: Key words
defs: Two identical molecules react to give a cation and an anion: 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
A molecule or ion that can donate or accept a proton, depending on its partner.

screens.text: Amphiprotic species can donate AND accept a proton. Which of these are amphiprotic? Pick all.
screens.why:
Step 1: an amphiprotic species needs an H⁺ to give AND a lone pair to take H⁺.
Step 2: H₂O → OH⁻ or H₃O⁺. HCO₃⁻ → CO₃²⁻ or H₂CO₃. H₂PO₄⁻ → HPO₄²⁻ or H₃PO₄.
Step 3: NO₃⁻ and CH₃COO⁻ have no acidic H to give: they only accept.
Step 4: HNO₃ is a strong acid: it only donates in water.
Answer: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, H₂PO₄⁻.
screens.clue: Look for species with a removable H AND room for one more.

screens.text: Amphiprotic H₂PO₄⁻: when it acts as a base, what does it become?
screens.why:
Step 1: a base ACCEPTS one H⁺.
Step 2: H₂PO₄⁻ + H⁺ → H₃PO₄.
Step 3: charge: −1 + 1 = 0.
Answer: H₃PO₄. HPO₄²⁻ is what forms when H₂PO₄⁻ acts as an acid.

screens.text: Autoionization: which equation shows the self-ionization of liquid ammonia?
screens.why:
Step 1: self-ionization needs two identical molecules and no other substance.
Step 2: one NH₃ gives H⁺ and becomes NH₂⁻.
Step 3: the other takes H⁺ and becomes NH₄⁺.
Answer: 2NH₃ ⇌ NH₄⁺ + NH₂⁻, just like 2H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
The option with H₂O is ammonia acting as a base in water, not self-ionization.
screens.clue: Same pattern as water, no water involved.

screens.text: Strongest base in a solvent: what is the strongest base that can exist in liquid ammonia?
screens.why:
Step 1: the solvent, NH₃, can give up an H⁺.
Step 2: any base stronger than NH₂⁻ takes H⁺ from NH₃.
Step 3: that reaction turns it into NH₂⁻ at once.
Answer: NH₂⁻. In the same way, OH⁻ is the strongest base in water.
screens.clue: Think of the solvent minus one H⁺.

en.text: Lewis defined acids and bases by electron pairs. A Lewis base donates an electron pair; a Lewis acid accepts one to form a bond. Look for a lone pair (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, Cl⁻) and an empty orbital (B in BF₃, metal ions, CO₂, H⁺). The Lewis idea is the broadest: every Brønsted–Lowry reaction is also a Lewis reaction.

am.text: ሉዊስ ቤዝ የኤሌክትሮን ጥንድ ይሰጣል፤ ሉዊስ አሲድ ይቀበላል። ይህ ትርጉም ከሦስቱ ሰፊው ነው።

screens.title: No proton moves
screens.ask: BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B–NH₃. No H⁺ moves. Is this an acid–base reaction?
opts: Yes: NH₃ shares its lone pair with B
screens.after:
B in BF₃ has only six valence electrons: it has room for one pair.
N in NH₃ has a lone pair.
N gives the pair to B and a new B–N bond forms.
No H⁺ moves, yet it is an acid–base reaction in the Lewis sense.
screens.best: Yes: NH₃ shares its lone pair with B

screens.title: Electron pairs
paras: Lewis base: donates an electron pair to form a bond.
Lewis acid: accepts an electron pair to form a bond.
B in BF₃ has only 6 valence electrons: it has room for a pair.
Look for a lone pair (base) and an empty orbital (acid).
Negative ions and molecules with lone pairs: bases. Cations and electron-poor molecules: acids.

screens.title: Three definitions, one inside another
screens.ask: Tap a circle. Then tap each reaction to see which definitions cover it.
rings: Acid accepts an electron pair; base donates one. The broadest idea.
Acid gives H⁺; base takes H⁺. Water is not needed.
Acid gives H⁺ in water; base gives OH⁻ in water. The narrowest idea.
numbers: H⁺ and OH⁻ in water. It fits all three definitions.
NH₃ takes H⁺ from water. No OH⁻ is released by NH₃, so it is not Arrhenius.
Proton transfer with no water. Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis, not Arrhenius.
No proton moves. Only the Lewis idea covers it.
Each NH₃ gives a lone pair to Ag⁺. Lewis only.

screens.title: Key words
defs: A species that accepts an electron pair to form a bond.
A species that donates an electron pair to form a bond.

screens.text: Find the Lewis acid (electron-pair acceptor) in BF₃ + NH₃ → F₃B–NH₃.
screens.why:
Step 1: find the lone pair: N in NH₃ has one. NH₃ is the base.
Step 2: find the empty orbital: B in BF₃ has only 6 valence electrons.
Step 3: B accepts the pair from N.
Answer: BF₃. F₃B–NH₃ is the product (the adduct).
screens.clue: Which atom has an empty orbital?

screens.title: Match each reaction with its Lewis acid
screens.why:
Step 1: in each reaction, find who brings a lone pair: OH⁻, Cl⁻, H₂O (twice) and CO are the bases.
Step 2: the partner that accepts the pair is the Lewis acid.
Step 3: H⁺ (no electrons), BCl₃ (B has 6 valence electrons), CO₂ (C is electron-poor).
Step 4: Ni and K⁺ accept lone pairs from CO and H₂O.
Check: each acid has room for a pair; each base has one to give.
screens.clue: Find the species with room for an electron pair.

screens.text: Find the Lewis base (electron-pair donor) in CaO + CO₂ → CaCO₃.
screens.why:
Step 1: CaO is Ca²⁺ and O²⁻.
Step 2: O²⁻ has lone pairs to give.
Step 3: the C atom of CO₂ accepts a pair: CO₂ is the Lewis acid.
Answer: CaO (its O²⁻) is the Lewis base. CaCO₃ is the product.
screens.clue: Which species has the lone pair?

screens.text: Lewis bases: which statement about them is NOT true?
opts: Lewis bases donate an electron pair
screens.why:
Step 1: a Lewis base donates an electron pair, so it must be electron-rich.
Step 2: water has two lone pairs on O, so water is a Lewis base.
Step 3: cations have lost electrons; they usually ACCEPT pairs (Lewis acids).
Answer: "Lewis bases are cationic" is NOT true.
screens.clue: Which species have spare electron pairs?

screens.text: Compare definitions: which is a Lewis acid but NOT a Brønsted–Lowry acid?
screens.why:
Step 1: a Brønsted–Lowry acid must have an H⁺ to give.
Step 2: HCl, NH₄⁺ and H₂O all have H⁺ to give.
Step 3: BF₃ has no H at all.
Step 4: but B in BF₃ accepts an electron pair.
Answer: BF₃ is a Lewis acid only.
screens.clue: A Brønsted–Lowry acid must have an H to give.

test.why:
Step 1: Brønsted–Lowry is about proton (H⁺) transfer.
Step 2: the acid GIVES the proton; the base takes it.
Answer: a proton donor.
"Electron-pair donor" is a Lewis base, not an acid.

test.text: Compare definitions: which is a Brønsted–Lowry base but not an Arrhenius base?
test.why:
Step 1: an Arrhenius base must release OH⁻ in water.
Step 2: NaOH, KOH and Ca(OH)₂ all release OH⁻: they are both kinds.
Step 3: NH₃ has no OH⁻; it takes H⁺ from water instead.
Answer: NH₃.

test.text: Conjugate pairs: what is the conjugate base of H₂SO₄?
test.why:
Step 1: a conjugate base has one FEWER H⁺.
Step 2: H₂SO₄ − H⁺ → HSO₄⁻.
Step 3: charge: 0 − 1 = −1.
Answer: HSO₄⁻. SO₄²⁻ is two steps away.

test.text: In H₂O + SO₃²⁻ ⇌ OH⁻ + HSO₃⁻, which product is the conjugate acid?
test.why:
Step 1: SO₃²⁻ takes H⁺ from water: it is the base.
Step 2: adding H⁺ to SO₃²⁻ gives HSO₃⁻.
Step 3: the conjugate acid is the base plus one H⁺.
Answer: HSO₃⁻. OH⁻ is the conjugate base of water.

test.text: Find the Lewis acid (electron-pair acceptor) in OH⁻ + CO₂ → HCO₃⁻.
test.why:
Step 1: OH⁻ has lone pairs on O: it is the Lewis base.
Step 2: the C atom of CO₂ is electron-poor and accepts the pair.
Step 3: a new C–O bond forms, giving HCO₃⁻.
Answer: CO₂.

notes.text: Exercise 1.1 a and c: the book's equations are unbalanced (2Br⁻, 2OH⁻). Correct: HBr + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Br⁻; NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻.
p.8: "CH₃COO⁻ is a strong base" is wrong; acetate is a weak base (Chart 1.1 lists it as weak). It is only stronger than Cl⁻.
p.4: the strong Group IIA hydroxides are usually Ca(OH)₂, Sr(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂ (Mg(OH)₂ is only slightly soluble).
Review Part I Q1 is missing "not": "a Brønsted–Lowry base but NOT an Arrhenius base" (answer NH₃).
